searchText: The risk is that people stop clearing storage because there is no financial incentive to do so anymore. Which will result in state growth. <@!301186049323958275> Im gonna try to pull some data on this, to see how much clearing is being done. What do you think of reduction vs. elimination of refund? <vbuterin> Yeah, the phrase "spam" is binary and moralistic ("let's blame those users doing things we think are not sufficiently worthy!") <vbuterin> It's definitely more correct to talk about externalities <vbuterin> I prefer the word "congestion" <vbuterin> It's a bit less technocratic than "externalities" <vbuterin> But describes the problem well <@!636212126939217941> I have, in the past, proposed removing gas refunds for basically the same reason you have here. The pushback is that we'll see even more state growth than we already do which is currently a top problem for Ethereum. I don't think a reduction would really help all that much. Gas tokens would still be profitable, just at a higher spread in gas price. Given we have seen a 500x spread, I don't think any reduction is going to do much. 🙂 I'm not personally convinced gas refunds are achieving the goal they set out to achieve. I have seen extremely little code that goes out of its way to clear data. It either clears data because it needs to set a value to 0, or it doesn't. Also, clearing data unnecessarily (just for the gas refund) results in more complexity in gas estimation, which often times is *worse* for dapp usability than just having a higher (but more stable) gas cost for a transaction. I have some code, for example, that I recently wrote that will probably end up using a constant time square root function instead of an efficient square root function just so I don't have to deal with gas limit variability. Side note: Would be cool if we had a mechanism to tell gas estimation tools that some function internal should be estimated to cost X gas, but without having to design the function to be constant gas. <@!301186049323958275> not sure i understand this last point You mean my side note? yes Not really related to your thing, just me lamenting. 🙂 It is a bit of a UX nightmare to have contract calls that consume different amounts of gas depending on state of the network at the time the transaction is executed. The most pathological case is when you have something like continuous interest calculation where the gas used changes every second depending how many 1 bits happen to be set in the current timestamp. The problem here is that gas estimators just run the transaction *now* and see how much gas it costs, and then use that as the gas estimate. There is no way for contract authors to give hints to gas estimators to say, "this thing should be estimated as costing X" (e.g., assume worst case scenario that all 1 bits in the timestamp are set). Again, unrelated to your thing. 🙂 > The pushback is that we'll see even more state growth than we already do which is currently a top problem for Ethereum. <@!301186049323958275> say refund is removed, and a contract is no longer used (dormant) and isn't cleared ofc because there's no incentive, it is really a burden on state? It adds no additional `compute` overhead on a syncing node .. or am i missing something? If data isn't zeroed out, then it stays in state forever, which means state grows at a faster rate than if state is zeroed out. The main issue right now isn't compute, it is state size. State doesn't currently fit into memory on most machines, which means state access sometimes goes to disk which is expensive. Also IIUC, due to the nature of Ethereum's state model, random access speed needs to be high, which means you basically *have* to use SSD storage. As state continues to grow, it continues to require larger and larger SSD drives. I personally run a server in the cloud and it is *very close* to the point where I have to decide to stop running an Ethereum node or bump up a cost tier which is pretty significant. > which means state access sometimes goes to disk which is expensive <@!301186049323958275> if I understood some of the recent Turbo-geth updates correctly, caching is much more improved, so this dormant contract costs mostly disk space. I could be wrong though Cc <@456226577798135808> I think getting turbo-geth strategies integrated into all major clients is a pretty long-term roadmap solution. To put it another way, we have a serious problem today (state growth) and removing gas refunds *may* make that problem worse. We have solutions to the state growth problem in the works (regenesis, stateless, turbogeth, etc.) but we need to be careful not to overly exacerbate the state growth problems until we actually have those solutions live. I'm playing a bit of devil's advocate here, I am weakly in favor of removing gas refunds today. Mainly because I don't *think* they actually (in the real world, with irrational humans and all that) incentivize the behavior they are intended to incentivize. However, if you believe that gas refunds *do* actually incentivize the behavior that we want then the state growth problem is the argument against removing them. Would be nice to know: the effect of removing gas refund is equivalent to raising the block gaslimit by X. Difficult to quantify i think Removing the refund would be equivalent to *reducing* the gas limit I believe. Since refunds make more space available in a block by reducing the gas used by a transaction. Though, I suppose you are thinking of the gas token killing aspect, since mining gas tokens consumes more gas than burning them. exactly I would gladly entertain the proposals for removing refunds. But, trying to be a pragmatic, I defer them to the time when we'd actually have bandwidth for those. The way Ethereum core dev organisation is structured right now, means that key core developers need to be developers and "politicians" at the same time, which takes a lot of time and energy. Therefore, I am now cautious of taking up proposals that have merit, but would divert my time from things I personally think would have greater and more lasting impact. At the same time, I am constantly thinking how to increase our dev bandwidth, and try to align my strategy with this goal. I know it does not sound very satisfying for you <@!636212126939217941> , sorry 🙂 In terms of dormant contracts taking only disk space. It is mostly true. What we realised is that unless you are storing the state database on HDD (with mechanical moving parts, and huge penalty for accessing data out-of-order), the inactive state does not have huge impact during tx replay, but there is still impact. But it does have impact when re-transmitting state snapshot over the network, obviously. I did not gather any stats, but my intuition tells me that refunds do very little to incentivise clearing the space. I also wrote about it in one of my State Rent proposals with the benefit of the hindsight, I should say that introducing refunds was a good idea, but perhaps implemented not in a best way. Refunds are tricky to use efficiently for "legitimate" purposes (expect some very simple cases where you create and self-destruct a contract within the same tx), and they are capped, but they have this side-effect of the gas token <@456226577798135808> do you have a list of the implementation changes to gas refunds you would suggest? I meant the changes that <@!636212126939217941> proposed - effectively making any gas refund equal to zero for destructing the contract and setting storage item to zero Implementation is likely trivial (changing 2 numbers), but the implications are potentially large If the change is small, why worry about core dev time if a non-core dev is willing to champion the change? That is, someone else does all of the EIP work, hard fork inclusion work, test generation work, etc. Is the concern just the overhead cost of switching? I am not worried about implementation time, I am worried about time we would spend as "politicians" arguing about this 🙂 I would be happy for this change to be implemented, even given the opposition of so-called "GasToken whales" and people who would like to use "Wisp" design pattern and from ENS, of course despite the opposition though, I do believe this change may contribute to solving a "higher order" problem at the expense of some people having to spend more gas unit for some operations. If at the end, the gas price drop 50%, then the argument for not doing it is moot but I do not have any evidence and confidence that this change would help reduce the gas price I actually think adding an exception for the wisp pattern is reasonable Basically, change the mechanics so that CREATE costs 7000 gas at the beginning, and then charges 25000 + 200 * length at creation time so if the init phase exits without creating that 25k is never charged Making those exceptions would make change more complicated, from "trivial" to "not so trivial". So I would use this argument - if there is some reasonable "evidence" that the usage of gas token and CHI makes the gas price problem much worse, then people using Wisp pattern will end up paying less fees if we cancel refunds 🙂 and then if the Wisp pattern is so important, we should probably create a dedicate primitive for it or something if it was up to me, I would just do it because why not 🙂 What I would do is bunch this up with the change that increases gas cost for stuff (EIP-2929 I believe), and do it as soon as possible, as the "Berlin" hardfork and then everything else (BLS, subroutines) after that it would also be a great way to ensure all the miners upgrade to the new tx pool handling in geth > and from ENS, of course <@456226577798135808> Does ENS use gas tokens? no, but they use self-destruct refunds quite a lot, though I am not sure they'll object to zeroing them > it would also be a great way to ensure all the miners upgrade to the new tx pool handling in geth <@456226577798135808> If these things were done quickly, I think it would be a good display to the community at large as well. but I would actually replace EIP-2929 with a much simpler version, which is trivial to implement I would remove all exemptions except for precompiles, and also would remove SSTORE changes Ah, sorry SSTORE modifications are required <vbuterin> The exemptions are required for viability imo <vbuterin> Specifically the cache map <vbuterin> A big reason why is that as I understand solidity checks codesize before calling <vbuterin> Which currently costs 800 * 2, and with the EIP would go up only to 2600, so quite a small increase <vbuterin> Whereas without the cache map it would be a crazy 5200 <vbuterin> Also, you'd need to exempt self-calling... <vbuterin> So may as well just "do it properly" Ok, I see, I do not see this change as trivial anymore perhaps it is best to just cancel refunds first 🙂 this is actually how it happens all the time, you get all excited about something, and then you find so many nuances, and then you go: "Oh, this is going to take some time...." 🙂 I think ☝️ is why engineers are notoriously bad at estimates. It is *sooo* easy to not consider the nuance and edge cases. I can’t see how this can resolve the gas price problem. If is a problem of state size, the solution is something inverse of removing the refund 😅 Nobody removes data onchain because is not a problem of them. If space is valuable to miners/validates Then the refund should be align with that To stop gastoken refund a % of the actual gas cost at time of deploy <@!568002278116687873> The problem is that we don't have any strong evidence that the refund is incentivizing the behavior we had hoped, and we have seen that it *does* incentivize behavior that is counter productive to the system running smoothly (gas tokens). Refunding 50% of something and I have to pay the rest is not a proper incentive to make a tx just to clean state I still have to pay to clean state > To stop gastoken refund a % of the actual
